plain grep beat semantic search.

Perplexity described how its agents work inside Projects last week. every project is a git repo. each agent gets its own short-lived sandbox and commits to a shared repository on S3, and fewer than 2% of submissions collide. the search layer is the part worth sitting with: the agents find things with plain ls and grep, and on financial document analysis that beat semantic search on answer accuracy, 63% to 37%.

two lessons in one setup. first, structure beats cleverness. a boring repo with a clear file layout let many agents work in parallel with almost no conflicts. second, retrieval an agent can reason about outperforms retrieval it has to trust. grep returns an exact match it can verify. an embedding returns "probably relevant."

the default that costs you: reaching for vector search and an orchestration framework before you have organised the files.

what I do: before any agent touches a codebase or a document set, I write the architecture rules first. folder layout, naming, what lives where, what the agent may change. agents follow structure extremely well and invent it badly.

the check: ask the agent where a given piece of logic lives. if it has to search semantically to answer, the structure isn't carrying its weight.

I use a prompt that sets exactly this up. it puts the model in the lead-architect seat and makes it follow your architecture rules before it writes code.

Perplexity reports fewer than 2% of agent submissions collide under that setup.

the architecture-first prompt, rules before code:

https://godofprompt.ai/prompt-library/build-full-stack-software-architectures
follow if you want agents that follow your structure instead of inventing their own.

Every added layer of complexity in an application makes it 10x harder to describe and make content on. 

Back in April I was making many videos on Codex. 

"Codex, OpenAI's version of Claude Code" 
"Codex, the desktop app on your computer"
"Codex, the super app that can do any CPU task"

Very, very easy to describe. 
Repeatable, and viral. 

This made it effortless to describe on short form or long from videos.

Then ChatGPT and Codex merged. 

Okay, now Codex is not an app. 
Codex is a feature inside ChatGPT. 

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT Desktop app"

Okay, now ChatGPT has "GPT Work"

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT desktop app that allows you to do coding tasks, and sometimes work tasks, some of those should be done inside GPT Work, which is kind of similar, but like different, depending on if you are using Cloud GPT Work, or local GPT work, in which case is alot closer to Codex, but still not quite the same. If you try and use the skills you created on Codex they won't work when doing a cloud GPT Work session but if it's a local session it will work."

We haven't even made it to Codex Cloud sessions, GPT Dots, and GPT Plugins yet. 

This goes for anyone building software. If you want to create an ecosystem of creators who talk about your product organically, you should aim for simplicity.

BTW not saying it was the wrong decision for OpenAI to merge them, i'm just saying for me it got much harder to describe with every new feature added.

月之暗面 10 月 23 日发布 Kimi K3.1 Pro，Kimi 网页版和 App、办公助手 Kimi Work、编程工具 Kimi Code 和 API 当天都能用。

官方说它是自家最强的开放权重模型，完整权重 11 月 4 日前放出。

K3.1 Pro 是在上一代 Kimi K3 基础上继续训练出来的，模型结构没换，多花了大量算力做强化学习，也就是让模型在几百个领域里反复做任务、按结果打分改进。

模型总共 2.8 万亿参数，处理每个 token 只动用其中约 1040 亿（token 是 AI 处理文字的单位，可以理解成文字碎片）。这种结构叫混合专家（MoE）：模型里有很多分工不同的“专家”小网络，每次只叫上一小部分干活，所以比同样大的普通模型算得快，但整个模型仍要全部装进内存。它一次能读 100 万 token，相当于一个中型代码仓库或几百页财报，也能看图和视频。

【和 Claude、GPT 比怎么样】

下面的成绩都来自月之暗面自己公布的对比表，对手是 Anthropic 的 Claude Opus 5.5、Claude Fable 5.1 和 OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Astra，所有模型开到最高推理强度。部分对手成绩是 Kimi 自己测的，内部测试外人无法复现。

写代码基本追平。

在命令行里完成真实开发任务的 Terminal-Bench 4.0，K3.1 Pro 65.7%，Opus 5.5 66.4%，GPT-6 Astra 58.2%；做大型软件项目的 SWE-Marathon，K3.1 Pro 51.7 分排第一，Opus 5.5 46.3。科学计算类的 Terminal-Bench Science 差距大，K3.1 Pro 38.1，GPT-6 Astra 68.1。

3D 建模稍逊。

K3.1 Pro 能直接写脚本操作 Blender、CAD 软件和 Unity、Unreal、Godot 游戏引擎，官方演示里做出了完整的 3D 游戏和能 3D 打印的台灯。在看几张渲染图、写 CAD 代码把零件还原出来的 BenchCAD 上，K3.1 Pro 92.7%，Opus 5.5 96.2%，GPT-6 Astra 95.9%。

金融是这次主打。

读真实财务文件、做多步计算的 OfficeQA Pro v2，K3.1 Pro 64.4 分排第一，Opus 5.5 62.2。Kimi 内部测试里，财务建模比 K3 高 7.2 分，写研究报告高 11.6 分。

推文说的“幻觉降低 65%”，来自 Kimi 内部一套专挑难题的事实核查测试：K3 说的每 100 个事实里有 23 个错的，K3.1 Pro 降到 8 个出头。同一测试里 Opus 5.5 是 15 个，GPT-6 Astra 是 5.5 个。官方注明这是压力测试，不代表日常使用的出错率。

【多少钱，能不能自己跑】

普通用户在 Kimi 网页版和 App 里就能用，免费用户能用多少官方没写。企业版默认关闭，要管理员手动开。

API 每百万 token 输入 2 美元、输出 10 美元，是 K3 价格的三分之二。Claude Opus 5.5 是输入 4 美元、输出 20 美元，贵一倍。快 2 到 3 倍的 Highspeed 版输入 4 美元、输出 20 美元，和 Opus 5.5 同价。API 账户要先充值至少 1 美元才能用。

开放权重是指模型文件公开，任何人都能下载，放在自己的服务器上运行、微调，数据不用经过月之暗面。但个人电脑跑不动：按 K3 采用的 4 位精度推算，光存放 2.8 万亿参数就要约 1.4TB 内存。许可证条款官方还没公布。

为了开放权重，月之暗面说训练时删掉了网络攻防相关的数据。同一套训练流程不删数据，内部漏洞利用测试能解 90.5% 的题，删了之后是 81.0%。官方称它的攻击能力仍落后于已经公开三个月以上的闭源顶级模型。

"But I think that answer almost always comes back to a set of tasks for you to go do. It might be, you should go call and book an appointment with a doctor, call and book an appointment with a specialist, go get these sets of labs, or go get this imaging done."

"While advice is abundant, you then are immediately stuck back with the realities of the current healthcare system."

"We've for a very long time felt like the best modality for that is a store. Everything else in your life, you search and browse the options available to you, you understand what they cost, you understand when they're available, and you go buy the thing."

"The time is right for something like this in healthcare because the bottleneck is no longer advice, the bottleneck is taking action on that advice."

Five years into his run as CEO, Andy Jassy has nearly tripled the size of AWS, grown Amazon's revenue by about 80%, and expects to spend $220 billion this year to win AI. Amazon's AI business hit a $25 billion run rate in three years, growing several hundred times faster than early AWS.

Jassy joins a16z's Ben Horowitz and Erik Torenberg to discuss the decisions behind that run, from rebuilding Amazon's fulfillment network after the pandemic to the AWS origin story.

They also cover why data centers became a political fight, Amazon's custom chips, its stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI, why inference needs to get 10x cheaper, AI's most underrated risk, and why every company will have to reinvent its products from scratch, plus Jassy's advice for anyone who's 18 today.

Amazon's AI business is growing several hundred times faster than AWS did, and it's driving a big part of Amazon's $220B investment this year. CEO Andy Jassy says they "haven't seen anything like it."

"In the first three years of this generative AI wave, our AI business in AWS is over $25 billion in run rate. So it's several hundred times faster."

"We've said this year in 2026, we expect to spend about $220 billion of CapEx."

"I remember being at a leadership team breakfast 15 years ago when we couldn't believe a telco company spent $50 billion in CapEx. We're like, 'How are they spending that much on CapEx?' So these numbers, they’re kind of mind-blowing numbers."

"Even spending $220 billion in CapEx this year, we're leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table. The thing that helps us here is that we have really good visibility into customer demand."

text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy on what AI means for the future of organizations: smaller teams, new jobs, and the ability to invent "much more expansively and much more quickly."

"I started at the company 29 years ago. I started as an assistant product manager, and I was the product manager for, I don't know, five products."

"When companies get successful and they get bigger... everybody becomes more specialized, and everybody accepts that that's the way you have to do business if you're building something big and successful, and it's not."

"And it's definitely not when you look at what's happening with AI."

"I think what it means for the future of organizations is, number one, we're gonna have fewer humans doing the work that they're doing today... You're not gonna have no people, but you're not gonna have as many humans as we've all thrown at scale as businesses have gotten bigger."

"There are gonna be different jobs and new jobs, some of which we know about, some of which we don't know about, that will arise as AI and robotics and space develop."

"I think you're gonna have smaller teams that have people who can work cross-functionally. They don't only own one sliver because the models are gonna be able to get them 80% of the way there... I think that every team will start at a much more advanced stage than we have in the past."

Five years into his run as CEO, Andy Jassy has nearly tripled the size of AWS, grown Amazon's revenue by about 80%, and expects to spend $220 billion this year to win AI. Amazon's AI business hit a $25 billion run rate in three years, growing several hundred times faster than early AWS.

Jassy joins a16z's Ben Horowitz and Erik Torenberg to discuss the decisions behind that run, from rebuilding Amazon's fulfillment network after the pandemic to the AWS origin story.

They also cover why data centers became a political fight, Amazon's custom chips, its stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI, why inference needs to get 10x cheaper, AI's most underrated risk, and why every company will have to reinvent its products from scratch, plus Jassy's advice for anyone who's 18 today.

text:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy's advice for young people: AI will help you "invent in ways that just weren't possible" before, and critical thinking and human judgment will remain your edge.

"You can't run away from it, and you can't wish it away. It's gonna be incredibly impactful in your life, in every experience that you try and use in your work... You need to learn about it. You need to educate yourself about it. You need to use it a lot. You need to try it."

"I don't think it replaces critical reasoning and thinking."

"If I think about business school as an example, you would get these three cases that you had to analyze every day, and you had to do a lot of reading, and you had to take notes, and you had to figure out what the key issues were... All that kind of goes away with AI."

"AI is gonna be able to kind of get everybody to that advanced starting spot much more quickly."

"The actual putting the dots and the pieces together, either to build a strategy or an approach or a plan or a new product or a new customer experience, I don't think AI is gonna do that for most people most of the time."

"I still think you're gonna need human judgment and ingenuity and invention and experimentation and thinking about how all the pieces come together to end up building amazing experiences and businesses."
